questions.question: What is the Gini impurity of a node containing 50% class A and 50% class B?
questions.explanation: Gini impurity is 1-(0.5 squared+0.5 squared)=0.5. A pure node has impurity zero.

questions.question: What is the entropy of a node whose examples all have the same class?
questions.explanation: A pure distribution has no class uncertainty, so its entropy is zero.

questions.question: How should a tree choose between candidate splits using information gain?
options: Choose the split with the largest parent impurity minus weighted child impurity
Choose the split with the deepest children
Choose the split with the largest number of distinct feature values
Choose the split that leaves every child exactly the same size
questions.explanation: Information gain measures the reduction in impurity after weighting each child by its sample fraction.

questions.question: Which setting is a pre-pruning control in the scratch tree?
questions.explanation: max_depth limits how far the tree can split before training finishes, reducing overly complex branches.

questions.question: Why do bootstrap samples and random feature subsets help a random forest?
options: They force every tree to use the same errors
They remove the need for labeled targets
They decorrelate trees so averaging reduces variance
They make each individual tree deeper and unbiased
questions.explanation: Different samples and features produce less-correlated trees; averaging their predictions stabilizes the ensemble.

questions.question: A categorical feature has hundreds of unique values. Why might MDI importance overrate it?
options: MDI ignores every feature with a numeric encoding
Permutation importance always assigns it zero
A high-cardinality feature cannot be used in a tree
Many possible split points make impurity reductions easy to find by chance
questions.explanation: Impurity-based importance favors features with many candidate splits. Permuting the feature and measuring the performance drop is a less split-search-dependent check.
